planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; unusually cold-hardy for a kaki-type persimmon and, like most Diospyros kaki cultivars, is self-fruitful and needs no second tree for pollination.

directions: Sheng is an astringent-type Asian persimmon, meaning the fruit is mouth-puckering and inedible while firm and must be allowed to soften completely to jelly-ripe before eating, at which point it turns rich, nutty, and very sweet. Fruit is notably large, flattened, and squarish with four lobes, ripening early in September through October and often holding well on the tree. The tree grows as a dwarf to semi-dwarf, upright, irregularly branched form with large glossy leaves, making it a good fit for smaller home orchards, and it is markedly more cold-tolerant than typical Asian persimmon cultivars, extending kaki growing into cooler zones than most non-astringent types can handle. Like other kaki persimmons it is self-fruitful and reliably productive once established.

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and does not require a second tree for pollination.

directions: Tecumseh was named and selected by Dr. Jim Shanks of the University of Maryland, likely from seed of the hardy astringent cultivar Great Wall, and shares that parent's cold-hardiness and reliable productivity. As an astringent-type persimmon it must fully soften before eating, but it is unusual for holding ripe fruit on the tree deep into winter, often into January or February, extending the harvest window well past most other cultivars. The fruit is good fresh, dried, or frozen, and the tree is long-lived, self-fertile, and notably resistant to common pests and diseases while tolerating drought once established. Its small stature makes it a practical choice for home orchards with limited space.

common_name: Miss Kim Persimmon (Compact Weeping Cold-Hardy Asian Persimmon)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to half-day sun; self-fertile and does not need a second tree for pollination.

directions: Miss Kim is a naturally compact, self-fertile Asian persimmon prized for its weeping form and long, tropical-looking foliage that turns deep red in fall, making it as much a landscape specimen as a fruit tree. It is an astringent-type cultivar, so the large, round, reddish-orange fruit must soften completely, becoming tender like a ripe tomato, before it loses its puckery tannins and turns sweet and flavorful. Miss Kim leafs out earlier than most other Asian persimmon cultivars and ripens early, beginning in October and continuing on the tree into the cooler months. It has also proven hardier than many kaki cultivars in cold snaps, and trees typically begin bearing within two to three years of planting.

common_name: Hiratanenashi Persimmon (Classic Flat Seedless Japanese Astringent Kaki)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; sets seedless fruit through parthenocarpy and does not need a pollinator, and in fact is grown without one commercially to avoid seed formation.

directions: Hiratanenashi, whose name translates roughly to flat and seedless, is a traditional Japanese cultivar formally recorded in the Shonai region of Yamagata Prefecture in 1887 and remains one of Japan's most widely grown persimmons. It is a strongly astringent, highly parthenocarpic type that reliably produces seedless, flattened fruit even without pollination, which is exactly why it is grown as a solo tree commercially. The juicy, somewhat watery flesh must be fully softened or artificially treated to remove astringency before eating; unripe fruit is unpalatable. Once treated or fully soft-ripe, the fruit is mild, sweet, and prized for fresh eating and drying.

common_name: Costata Persimmon (Ribbed Seedless European-Grown Astringent Kaki)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; self-fertile and sets seedless fruit without a second tree.

directions: Costata is a vigorous astringent-type persimmon cultivar widely grown in European orchards, producing distinctively ribbed, seedless orange fruit. The flesh is tender and melting once fully ripe, losing its astringency completely as the fruit softens, but is puckery and unpleasant if eaten while still firm. Fruit ripens in October and is considered an early-season cultivar among astringent kaki types. The tree is a strong, reliable grower and, like most Diospyros kaki, is self-fertile and productive without a pollinator.

common_name: Prairie Sun American Persimmon (Cold-Hardy Seedless Early-Ripening Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil; self-fertile and sets seedless fruit without a pollinator.

directions: Prairie Sun, designated Claypool A-33, is a cold-hardy American persimmon selection bred by Jim Claypool and rated hardy to roughly -25F, well beyond the needs of most Southern growers but a mark of the tree's overall vigor and reliability. It is self-fertile, setting abundant crops of seedless, firm, yellow-orange fruit without a second tree, though fruit is astringent until fully soft-ripe, at which point it turns sweet and flavorful. Prairie Sun is one of the earlier-ripening American persimmon selections, with harvest typically beginning in late September to October, and the tree can be kept compact at 10-12 feet with regular pruning. Established trees tolerate heat, drought, and a wide range of soils with minimal care.

common_name: Valeene Beauty American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Precocious Indiana Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; like most named American persimmon selections, sets fruit parthenocarpically without needing a pollinator.

directions: Valeene Beauty, also recorded as Claypool I-94, is an Indiana-origin selection from a cross of Mitchellena and Early Golden made by James Claypool. It is notably precocious and a regular heavy producer, bearing large fruit 2.25 to 2.5 inches across that is low in fiber and high in pulp compared to many wild-type persimmons. As with all Diospyros virginiana cultivars, fruit is astringent and unpalatable until it softens fully, after which it becomes rich and sweet. The tree has an upright growth habit and can be pruned to hold it at 15 to 20 feet, tolerating the heat, drought, and variable soils typical of native persimmon once established.

common_name: C-100 American Persimmon (Large-Fruited Low-Speck Claypool Selection)

planting.note: Plant a grafted bare-root or container tree in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil, pH 6.0-7.0, in full sun; sets fruit parthenocarpically and does not need a pollinator.

directions: C-100 is a named American persimmon selection bred by the late James Claypool, valued by growers because its fruit contains few or no of the black flecks in the pulp that mar many seedling persimmons, an important quality trait for fresh and processed fruit alike. Its orange-red fruit resembles the well-known Morris Burton cultivar in appearance and flavor but runs larger, with excellent sweetness once fully soft-ripe; like all American persimmons it is astringent and inedible until then. Beyond fruit quality, C-100 offers strong landscape value, with dark green summer foliage that turns vivid red and yellow in autumn. The tree is cold-hardy and easily grown in full sun on a wide range of soils.
